extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy and aesthetics (readers of Kant)
extracted.subtask_description: Framework for forming and justifying aesthetical judgements (judgements of taste) about beauty and the sublime, following Kant’s Critique of Judgment. Focuses on what such judgements claim (universality, necessity), their grounds (subjective purposiveness, free play of faculties), and how they relate to communicability and social interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim to universal assent (subjective universality)
rubrics_metrics.description: A judgement of taste determines its object in respect of satisfaction (its beauty) with an accompanying claim for the assent of every one; e.g. saying 'this flower is beautiful' asserts its proper claim to satisfy every one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This universality is not objective (grounded in concepts) but a subjective claim: the judgement is singular yet presumes a validity 'for every one'. Examples: the flower (beauty vs smell), the distinction that beauty claims universal agreement even though based on a feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Autonomy of taste (judge by oneself)
rubrics_metrics.description: Taste claims autonomy: the subject should judge by himself, a priori, without needing to consult the judgements or satisfactions of others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid heteronomy (making the judgements of others the determining grounds). Example: the young poet who will not be dissuaded by public judgement; imitation vs following as legitimate influence. Exercise/sharpening of taste may later change one's judgement but not because others dictate it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Not determinable by grounds of proof (no demonstrative rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: The judgement of taste is not determinable by grounds of proof: neither empirical evidence (agreement of others) nor a priori conceptual proofs can force assent to a judgement of beauty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics' rules and enumerated ingredients (Batteux, Lessing) cannot compel assent if the aesthetic feeling differs. Analogies: tasting food — listing ingredients doesn't determine liking. Therefore, rules may inform or correct but cannot serve as decisive logical proofs for taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: No objective principle of Taste possible
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no principle under which we could subsume the concept of an object and infer by syllogism that the object is beautiful. Beauty is not a concept of the object and the judgement of taste is not cognitive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pleasure in taste is immediate in the act of judging; attempts to derive a universally applicable formula for beauty are impossible. The Critique of Taste instead seeks to explain the faculties (Imagination and Understanding) whose interplay grounds the feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taste as subjective (aesthetic, not cognitive)
rubrics_metrics.description: A judgement of taste is an aesthetic (non-cognitive) judgement: it binds pleasure to the mere act of judging a form, prior to concepts, and is therefore singular though it claims universal validity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish aesthetic judgements from cognitive ones: the former do not subsume representations under concepts but rest on a feeling tied to the representation of form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of taste = subjective principle of Judgement (free play harmony)
rubrics_metrics.description: The principle of taste rests on the subjective formal condition of Judgement: the free play and reciprocal harmony of Imagination (free schematising of intuition) and Understanding (conformity to law), felt as purposiveness of the representation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beauty arises when the Imagination in its freedom harmonises with the Understanding in its conformity to law, producing a felt pleasure. Taste subsumes the faculty of intuitions under the faculty of concepts only insofar as this free-harmony is perceived.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judgements of taste are synthetical with an a priori claim
rubrics_metrics.description: Judgements of taste are synthetical because they add a feeling of pleasure (not a cognitive predicate) to the representation; yet they assert an a priori universal validity (they desire to be regarded as necessary).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the double logical peculiarity: (1) a priori universal validity not based on concepts, (2) necessity that nevertheless does not rest on an a priori proof by concepts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deduction/justification via presupposed common subjective conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: The legitimacy of a judgement of taste (its claim to universal assent) is justified by presupposing the same subjective conditions of Judgement in all subjects — i.e., by deducing that the harmonious play of faculties is a condition we can reasonably impute to every one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This Deduction does not establish objective concepts but shows that we may validly assume the subjective conditions we find in ourselves in others; difficulties remain in subsumption but do not annul the claim to universal assent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communicability of feeling as criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Taste is the faculty of judging a priori of the communicability of feelings bound up with a representation (without mediation of a concept); communicability — whether a feeling can be assumed to be shareable by others — grounds the claim to universality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate between kinds of feelings: some sensations (sense-pleasures) are not universally communicable; the feeling relevant to taste must be one tied to the formal harmony of cognitive faculties and thus presumptively communicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish types of pleasure (criteria for communicability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pleasures differ in how communicable they are: (a) pleasure of enjoyment (sense-based) is empirical and not universally communicable; (b) moral pleasure requires concepts and is communicable via Reason; (c) pleasure in the Sublime involves rational contemplation and presupposes a moral/supersensible feeling; (d) pleasure in the Beautiful is a pleasure of mere reflection tied to free play of faculties and is communicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these distinctions to evaluate whether a pleasure can legitimately be imputed to everyone. Example: smell may please one and cause another pain (not communicable); beauty's pleasure is tied to faculties common to cognition and so is more likely communicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taste as sensus communis (communal sense)
rubrics_metrics.description: Taste can be called sensus communis: a faculty of judgement which, in reflection, takes account a priori of the mode of representation of all other men — comparing one’s judgement with the possible judgements of others and abstracting from private conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To exercise sensus communis, one 'puts oneself in the place of any other man', abstracts from personal sensations or charm, and attends to the formal features of the representation. This supports the universality-claim of aesthetic judgements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maxims for common human understanding (practical rules for fair aesthetic judgement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Three maxims: 1) think for oneself (unprejudiced thought); 2) put oneself in the place of every one else (enlarged thought); 3) always think consistently (consecutive thought).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These maxims help avoid prejudice and heteronomy in judgement: the first guards against passivity, the second against parochialism, the third integrates both into consistent reflection. They are practical heuristics for exercising sensus communis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical interest in the Beautiful (social dimension)
rubrics_metrics.description: Although a pure judgement of taste must have no determining interest, an empirical interest can be indirectly combined: the Beautiful empirically interests only in society, because sociability inclines humans to communicate pleasure and to value objects that facilitate shared satisfaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating beauty in social contexts, account for the function of taste in sociability and civilisation (ornamenting, refinement). However, this social interest is not the determining ground of pure aesthetic judgement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of mistaking charm or emotion for form (avoid conflating matter with form)
rubrics_metrics.description: A correct aesthetic judgement must not mistake matter (sensuous charm, emotion) for form (the formal purposiveness that grounds beauty); error in subsumption under the principle of taste often comes from such confusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique and self-scrutiny can correct such mistakes: the judge should distinguish empirical charm from the formal relation between imagination and understanding that produces the aesthetic pleasure claimed to be universal.
